questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Comparative advantage from labour requirements
questions.learningObjective: identify which country should specialise from unit labour requirements
questions.stem: With one unit of labour, country A can produce 4 units of cloth or 2 units of food; country B can produce 1 unit of cloth or 1 unit of food. On comparative advantage grounds, what should each country make?

options.text: B should make cloth and A should make food, because one unit of cloth costs B 0.5 units of food but costs A 1
options.misconception: divides each country's labour requirement by the other country's figure, which inverts both opportunity costs

options.text: A should make cloth and B should make food, because one unit of cloth costs A 0.5 units of food but costs B 1
A should make both goods while B should make food, since A is the more productive producer of both and so gains nothing from trade
options.misconception: treats productivity superiority as a reason to stay unspecialised, which is the claim the cost argument refutes

options.text: Neither country should specialise, since the labour required per unit differs between the two countries
options.misconception: reads a difference in labour productivity as evidence that specialisation cannot pay

questions.explanation: The opportunity cost of a unit of a good is the labour spent on it divided by the labour each unit of the other good consumes, and the comparison is always within a country. In A one unit of cloth takes a quarter of a unit of labour, and that quarter could have made half a unit of food, so cloth costs A 0.5 food. In B one unit of cloth takes a whole unit of labour, which could have made 1 unit of food, so cloth costs B 1 food. A has the lower cost of cloth and B the lower cost of food, and A is also the more productive producer of both goods, since a quarter of a unit of labour makes a unit of cloth in A against a whole unit in B, which is the separate statement that the cost argument does not rest on.
questions.hint: Convert each country's labour per unit of cloth into units of food forgone, then compare the two countries.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The autarky relative price
questions.learningObjective: compute the autarky relative price of a good from labour requirements
questions.stem: One unit of labour can be used to make 3 units of cloth or 9 units of food in this country. With no trade between countries, what is the relative price of one unit of cloth in units of food?

options.text: 9 units of food, because 9 is the number of units of food one unit of labour can make
options.misconception: quotes the food output per worker instead of converting the labour cost of cloth into food

options.text: 0.33 units of food, which is the labour one unit of cloth takes expressed in units of labour
options.misconception: reports the labour requirement per unit without converting it into forgone food output

options.text: 3 units of food, because the labour a unit of cloth takes could have made 3 units of food
0.11 units of food, which is the labour one unit of food takes expressed in units of labour
options.misconception: inverts the calculation by using the labour cost of the other good as the price of this one

questions.explanation: One unit of cloth absorbs one third of a unit of labour, and that third of a unit of labour could have turned out 3 units of food, since 9 times one third is 3. So the internal exchange rate set by production cost is 3 units of food for one unit of cloth, which is also 9 divided by 3. Two routes agree: taking the ratio of the two output rates, 9 over 3, or taking the labour per unit of cloth and multiplying it by the food rate, one third times 9. Reading the answer as 9 would confuse the rate of food output per worker with the price of cloth, and reading it as one third would give the labour cost without converting it into food.
questions.hint: Work out what the labour used for one unit of cloth could have produced instead.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Real income under autarky and under free trade
questions.learningObjective: compare real income in autarky and at world prices for a specialised country
questions.stem: A country can produce 3 units of cloth or 9 units of food per unit of labour. With no trade it makes 3 units of cloth per unit of labour; with free trade at a world price of 2 units of food per unit of cloth it makes 9 units of food per unit of labour and trades. Measured in units of cloth per unit of labour, what happens to real income?

options.text: It rises from 3 to 4.5 units of cloth, an increase of one half, but only because the country's purchases move the world price
options.misconception: attributes the whole gain to market power, which a small country gets at the same world price

options.text: It rises from 3 to 9 units of cloth, because a country can always consume the good it is most efficient at producing
options.misconception: values the food output at the autarky price of cloth rather than at the world price it can actually obtain

options.text: It falls from 3 to 2 units of cloth, because a world price of 2 units of food is a worse deal than the internal price of 3
options.misconception: reads the world price as if it were a quantity of cloth obtainable rather than a price

options.text: It rises from 3 to 4.5 units of cloth, an increase of one half, which is the ratio of the world price to the autarky price

questions.explanation: With no trade, the country spends one unit of labour on cloth and gets 3 units of it, so real income measured in cloth is 3. With trade it spends the labour on food, gets 9 units of food, and sells them at 2 units of food per cloth, so it can buy 9 over 2, which is 4.5 units of cloth. The gain is 4.5 divided by 3, or 1.5, and that factor is exactly the ratio of the world price of cloth, 2, to the autarky price of 3, because in this one-export model all of the country's labour sells at the world price. Nothing in the calculation depends on the country moving the world price, since the world price is the same for a small and a large country; what market power changes is the price itself, not the arithmetic.
questions.hint: Convert the food output into cloth at the world price, then divide by the autarky figure.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The terms of trade as a multiplier of real income
questions.learningObjective: state why the terms of trade multiplies real income for a specialised exporter
questions.stem: In a one-export model a country spends all of its labour on a single good, so its wage is that good's world price divided by the labour each unit takes. Why does the terms of trade, rather than output, decide how much of the gain from trade the country keeps?

answer.exemplar: If the country spends all of its labour making one good, the whole of its labour income is the price of that good times the output per worker, so real income is exactly the world price times the output per worker. The terms of trade is the ratio of the price of the export to the price of the import, so once the country is specialised the real income of a worker moves one for one with that ratio and with nothing else. A worker who can make 3 units of an export, priced at 2 units of import each, earns 6 units of import; at a price of 1.5 the same worker earns 4.5, and income has fallen by a quarter while nothing about the plant, the skills or the effort has changed. That is why an adverse terms of trade can undo a gain from trade entirely, and why a country with one dominant export is more exposed to it than a country that sells a varied basket.

questions.explanation: Real income for a specialised exporter is the product of the export price and labour productivity, so the exchange rate between the two goods, which is the terms of trade, is the single number that scales it. Output is already pinned at its maximum when the country has specialised, so there is no second source of growth to fall back on. The corollary is that the gain from trade is a price gain, not a quantity gain, and it can be reversed by a price move that has nothing to do with domestic policy or domestic productivity.
questions.hint: Ask what the country's labour income is worth when only one good is produced.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: A fall in the price of imports and real income
questions.learningObjective: compute the real income gain from a fall in import prices using the export share
questions.stem: A small country's output is 1,000 units, of which 300 are exported and 300 are imported, with domestic prices unchanged. The price of its exports is unchanged and the price of its imports falls 10 percent. As a percentage of the initial level of real income, how much does real income rise?

options.text: 10 percent, because the price of imports has fallen 10 percent and every unit of output is now cheaper
options.misconception: applies the import price change to the whole of output rather than to the traded share of it

options.text: 30 percent, because the import bill falls by 30 and that is the whole of the gain to the country
options.misconception: reports the saving on the import bill in money terms without dividing by the real income it is measured against

options.text: 3 percent, because the terms of trade rise 10 percent and only the exported 30 percent of output is priced at them
0.3 percent, because the exported share of output is 0.30 and the 10 percent price change has already been used up
options.misconception: quotes the export share as though it were the gain, with no price change applied to it at all

questions.explanation: The terms of trade, the export price over the import price, rises by 10 percent, and for a country that exports 300 of its 1,000 units of output the real income gain is that 10 percent applied to the export share: 0.30 times 10, which is 3 percent. The second route is the import bill, which falls from 300 to 270, so the country's real purchasing power rises by 30 against a base of 1,000, again 3 percent. Reading 10 would apply the price change to the whole of output rather than to the traded part, and reading 30 would report the change in the bill in money terms without dividing by the level of real income it is measured against.
questions.hint: The terms of trade gain counts only the traded share of output; check it against the saving on the import bill.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Consumption outside the production possibility frontier
questions.learningObjective: explain how trade lets a country consume outside its production possibility frontier
questions.stem: A country cannot produce more cloth and food together than its resources allow, yet it can consume a bundle that lies outside its own production possibility frontier. What makes that possible?

options.text: A country can consume beyond its frontier because it may use up its capital stock faster than it replaces it
options.misconception: supplies consumption beyond the frontier by drawing down capital, which is a temporary and finite source

options.text: Foreign goods enter the consumption possibilities at the world prices, so the consumption frontier lies outside the production frontier
A country can consume beyond its frontier because its production frontier is drawn for nominal output rather than real output
options.misconception: suggests the frontier is mislabelled and that correcting the label would create the extra goods

options.text: A country cannot consume outside its frontier at all, so the claim must rest on a different definition of output
options.misconception: denies the possibility outright and therefore rules out every case where trade is possible

questions.explanation: The production possibility frontier is built from the country's own resources and technology, so it bounds what can be made at home. Consumption possibilities are bounded by what can be bought, and once trade is possible the country faces a budget line set by world prices rather than only by its own costs, and that line lies outside the production frontier because the world is producing the goods it is short of. The distinction is why a country can be at full employment in production and still consume a bundle it could not produce, and why the constraint that binds in production does not bind in consumption.
questions.hint: Ask what prices govern the choice of a consumption bundle once imports are available.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Reciprocal demand and the terms of trade
questions.learningObjective: explain how reciprocal demand shapes the terms of trade in a two-country model
questions.stem: In a two-country model the world price of a good has to lie between the two autarky prices. What decides where inside that range it settles, and why does that matter for the division of the gains from trade?

answer.exemplar: The price settles where the quantity of the good each country demands at that price equals the quantity the other supplies, and the trade volumes are endogenously determined because the two countries' export goods are each other's import goods. The larger the share of world demand that one country brings to a good, the more its demand curve shifts out and the further the price moves towards the other country's autarky price, which is why the country with a small market typically has the steeper export supply curve and gets the better terms of trade. This is reciprocal demand: each country's size in the world market is a source of bargaining power that is independent of its technology. The division of the gain therefore cannot be read off the two autarky prices alone; the world price is the only place it is written down.

questions.explanation: The world price is pinned by market clearing rather than by either country's costs, and the conditions that do the pinning are the two countries' import demands and export supplies, which is the reason the price depends on how large each market is. A country that is small relative to the world is a price taker, so its terms of trade are given and its gain is the difference between that price and its own cost; a large country moves the price itself. Any argument about the division of the gains that cites only production costs is leaving out the demand side of the market.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be equal for the price to clear both markets.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: An export price shock and real income
questions.learningObjective: compute the real income loss from a fall in the export price
questions.stem: A small country exports 250 of its 1,000 units of output, and its import prices do not change. Its export price falls 12 percent for a year while output and volumes are unchanged. What is the change in real income as a percentage of its initial level, and what is the change in the size of the export sector measured in the same units?

options.text: Real income falls 3 percent, and the value of exports falls 30, which is 3 percent of output
Real income falls 12 percent, and the value of exports falls 30, because the whole of output is sold at the new price
options.misconception: applies the export price fall to the whole of output rather than to the exported quarter of it

options.text: Real income falls 6 percent, and the value of exports falls 30, because the terms of trade loss counts the same 3 percent twice
options.misconception: double counts a single terms of trade loss in the level of output and again in the export bill

options.text: Real income rises 3 percent, and the value of exports falls 30, because a cheaper export buys more foreign goods in return
options.misconception: reverses the sign, which is what a fall in the price of imports would do but not a fall in the price of exports

questions.explanation: Only the exported quarter of output changes price, so the loss in real income is 0.25 of output times 12 percent, which is 3 percent of the initial level. In money terms the export bill falls from 250 to 220, a fall of 30, and 30 divided by 1,000 is again 3 percent, so the two routes agree. The direction matters: a fall in the export price is a terms of trade loss, and since the import price is unchanged it cannot be offset by cheaper imports, which is what makes an export price shock different from a fall in the general price level. A rise in real income would need the price of imports to fall, not the price of exports.
questions.hint: Apply the price change to the exported share only, then check it against the fall in the export bill.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The factor content of a trade flow
questions.learningObjective: compute the factor content of an export from input coefficients
questions.stem: Making one unit of an export needs 2 units of labour and uses no capital. Making one unit of the imported good needs 3 units of labour. The country exports 40 units and imports 10 units in a year. How many units of labour does that trade flow release, relative to producing the same goods at home?

options.text: 110 units, since the exports use 80 and the imports use 30 and the two contents are added together
options.misconception: adds the labour embodied in imports to that embodied in exports instead of netting them

options.text: 80 units, counting only the labour used in the exported goods and ignoring the imported goods
options.misconception: omits the labour embodied in the imports that the exports displace

options.text: 30 units, counting only the labour used in the imported goods and ignoring the exported goods
options.misconception: reports the imported labour content alone and ignores the exported content that offsets it

options.text: 50 units, since the exports use 80 and the imports would have used 30, and 80 minus 30 is 50

questions.explanation: The export uses 40 times 2, or 80, units of labour and the imports use 10 times 3, or 30, so the trade flow releases 80 minus 30, which is 50 units of labour. Valued at a wage of 20 an hour, the labour embodied in the 40 exported units is 1,600 and in the 10 imported units is 600, so net exports carry 1,000 of labour content, and 1,000 divided by 20 is the 50 hours found the other way. The two contents have to be valued at the same wage before they can be subtracted, since they are otherwise measured in different goods.
questions.hint: Multiply each volume by its labour coefficient, then take the difference.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Factor price equalisation
questions.learningObjective: state what factor price equalisation predicts and the conditions it needs
questions.stem: In the factor content model of trade, two countries with different technologies can end up with the same wage rate and the same rate of return on capital. What must be assumed for that prediction to hold?

options.text: Each country must specialise completely in the goods it produces relatively cheaply, and goods and factors must be tradable or produced with the same technology
Only the wage rates must equalise, because the return on capital is fixed by the world stock of capital
options.misconception: equalises only the variable factor and treats the return on capital as given rather than as an equilibrium price

options.text: The countries must have identical technology, since otherwise the factor content of the two goods differs
options.misconception: requires identical technology, which is the assumption the theory uses in order to avoid it

options.text: The prediction holds whenever the number of traded goods exceeds the number of factors being compared
options.misconception: states a counting condition on the number of goods, which is not what limits the result

questions.explanation: The theory works by noting that the price of a good equals the wages and returns embodied in it, so if the two countries produce different goods with different factor contents and complete specialisation follows, the two price equalities pin down both factor prices. Complete specialisation is what removes the third equation that would otherwise allow a wedge between the factor prices, and the assumption about tradability or identical technology removes the reason for the goods prices to differ. Equal factor prices would then mean that a mobile factor earns the same everywhere, which is why the result is described as a knife-edge property of the assumptions rather than an empirical regularity.
questions.hint: Ask how many price equations there are and how many factor prices they must pin down.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: A specific factors model and sectoral employment
questions.learningObjective: state the employment prediction of a rise in the price of a traded good under specific factors
questions.stem: In a model with one mobile factor, labour, and one factor specific to each of two sectors, the price of a sector's output rises. Which of the following does the model predict?

options.text: Labour moves into the sector whose price rose and both specific factors gain, because the demand for both outputs must have risen
options.misconception: predicts a rise in every factor price, which would raise the cost of both goods at once

options.text: Labour leaves the sector whose price rose, so that the more profitable sector can raise its factor price without attracting labour
options.misconception: sends labour away from the sector whose product has become more valuable, which is the wrong direction

options.text: Labour moves into the sector whose price rose, the return to its specific factor rises, and the return to the other specific factor falls
Neither factor price changes, because a price change in one sector cannot be transmitted across a closed economy
options.misconception: rules out intersectoral factor mobility, which is the assumption the model is built on

questions.explanation: With labour mobile and one specific factor in each sector, a rise in the price of one sector's output raises that sector's revenue per unit of its own specific factor, so the price of that factor rises, and labour flows in to exploit the difference until the wage is equal in both sectors. The other sector then faces a higher wage with no offsetting revenue, so its specific factor loses. The prediction is that the specific factor in the expanding sector gains and the other loses, which is a distributional statement about who bears the cost of a terms of trade change rather than a statement that output expands.
questions.hint: Ask which factor cannot move between the two sectors, and what happens to its price when its sector's price rises.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The relative wage and relative factor intensity
questions.learningObjective: infer the factor intensity of a sector from the direction of the relative wage change
questions.stem: In the specific factors model, the price of the tradable good rises. Which statements about the labour intensity of the two sectors and about the real wage of the workers who move are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: The sector whose price rises employs labour intensively relative to its specific factor, so its demand for labour rises with the price
The workers who move into the expanding sector must have a lower wage there than in the sector they left, or the move would not have been worth making
The real wage of every worker in the economy rises, since a higher goods price raises the purchasing power of any given nominal wage
options.misconception: assumes the nominal wage rises with the goods price, which is the condition the model rules out

options.text: The real wage of the workers who move rises, because they are now employed in the more productive sector

questions.explanation: The expanding sector gains only if the value of its output per unit of the specific factor rises, which is what a rise in its output price does, and the more labour it uses the more of that gain reaches workers. Labour moves because the nominal wage is the same in both sectors, so the real wage is higher where the goods price is higher, and a worker who moves is therefore better off, not worse. The fourth statement is the one the model forbids: if the nominal wage rose with the price of goods, the real wage would be unchanged everywhere and the move would be arbitrary, so equilibrium requires the money wage not to rise with the goods price.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be true of the money wage for labour to want to move, and which sector uses labour intensively.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: A tariff on the imports of a small country
questions.learningObjective: identify the four effects of a tariff in a small importing country
questions.stem: A small country imposes a tariff on an imported good. Which of the following are consequences on its own domestic markets? Select all that apply.

options.text: The domestic price rises by the tariff, so domestic consumption falls and domestic production rises
Foreign producers necessarily lose the whole of their export revenue, since every unit taxed is no longer sold
options.misconception: assumes a tariff eliminates exports from the country imposing it, which is what a quota would do

options.text: Government revenue is the tariff multiplied by the volume of imports that is still bought
The welfare loss exceeds government revenue, because part of the revenue is offset by lost gains from trade

questions.explanation: The tariff raises the domestic price, so consumers buy less and domestic producers make more, and the gap between the two is the volume of imports that remains and on which revenue is raised. Part of that revenue is a transfer to producers and part is a transfer to the fiscal authority, but the losses to consumers exceed those transfers, and the excess is the deadweight loss, made up of the output misallocated towards the high cost domestic producer and the consumption forgone where consumers valued the good more than it cost to import. The fourth claim would only hold if the tariff were so large as to stop imports altogether, which is a quota set to zero.
questions.hint: Follow the price change through the three domestic demand and supply responses.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Tariff revenue and the deadweight loss
questions.learningObjective: compute tariff revenue and the deadweight loss from supply and demand responses
questions.stem: A small country imports a good at a world price of 10. At that price domestic consumers buy 70 units a year and domestic producers make 40, so imports are 30. A tariff of 25 percent is imposed, and at the new domestic price of 12.50 consumers buy 60 and producers make 45, so imports are 15. What revenue does the tariff raise, and what is the total deadweight loss? Give the two amounts in the same money units.

options.text: Revenue of 75 and a deadweight loss of 18.75, because the 2.5 wedge is applied to the volume imported before the tariff
options.misconception: applies the price wedge to the pre-tariff volume of 30 rather than to the 15 units still imported

options.text: Revenue of 37.5 and a deadweight loss of 6.25, counting only the units shifted to the dearer domestic producer
options.misconception: counts the production distortion and leaves out the consumption distortion from the same price rise

options.text: Revenue of 37.5 and a deadweight loss of 56.25, treating the whole of the revenue as a loss to the country
options.misconception: treats revenue raised domestically as a net loss, ignoring that it is a transfer to the fiscal authority

options.text: Revenue of 37.5 and a deadweight loss of 18.75, made up of 6.25 on production and 12.5 on consumption

questions.explanation: The tariff per unit is a quarter of 10, that is 2.5, and revenue is that wedge times the imports that survive, 15, giving 37.5. The deadweight loss is the sum of two triangles, each with a height of 2.5: the production distortion is half times 2.5 times the 5 units of extra domestic output, which is 6.25, and the consumption distortion is half times 2.5 times the 10 units of forgone consumption, which is 12.5, so 18.75 in total. The check that the two routes agree is 37.5 plus 18.75, which is 56.25, and that is the amount by which consumers are worse off before the revenue is taken into account, which is exactly the figure the last option mistakes for the deadweight loss.
questions.hint: Revenue is the wedge times post-tariff imports; the loss is two triangles, both with height equal to the wedge.

questions.topic: A tariff in a large country
questions.learningObjective: compute the terms of trade gain and the net income effect of a tariff in a large country
questions.stem: A large country imports a good. Its domestic demand is 500 minus 100 times the domestic price and its domestic supply is 200 plus 100 times that price, and foreign producers supply 400 times the world price minus 300, so at a world price of 1 the domestic price is 1 and imports are 100. A 20 percent tariff is imposed, so the domestic price is 1.2 times the world price. What is the gain in the terms of trade, and what is the net effect on the country's income?

options.text: A deadweight loss of 1.56 and a net gain of 3.13, since a tariff distorts trade and the gain it does produce is the loss
options.misconception: reports the distortion as the terms of trade gain, which is the opposite of what a large country obtains

options.text: A terms of trade gain of 4.69 and a net gain of 3.13, after subtracting a deadweight loss of 1.56 from the gain
A terms of trade gain of 4.69 and a net gain of 6.25, because the price fall is a gain and nothing offsets it
options.misconception: adds the distortion to the terms of trade gain instead of subtracting it, so the two are double counted

options.text: A terms of trade gain of 4.69 and a net gain of 4.69, because a large country's tariff faces no quantity response
options.misconception: suppresses the quantity response, which is what a large country's own demand and supply do produce

questions.explanation: Solving the two curves together, imports fall from 100 to 75 and the world price falls from 1 to 0.9375, so the country buys 75 units for what used to cost 100. The terms of trade gain is the new volume times the fall in the world price, 75 times 0.0625, that is 4.6875. The two triangles are 0.78125 each, since the domestic price rose 0.125 while production rose 12.5 and consumption fell 12.5, so the deadweight loss is 1.5625 and 4.6875 less 1.5625 is 3.125. The consumer and producer surpluses confirm it: the loss to consumers is 49.22 and the gain to producers 38.28, and with revenue of 14.06 the net is minus 49.22 plus 38.28 plus 14.06, which is 3.12.
questions.hint: Solve the two curves for the new world price and import volume, then take the terms of trade gain less the two triangles.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The effective rate of protection
questions.learningObjective: compute the effective rate of protection from a final good tariff and an input tariff
questions.stem: A finished good sells for 100 at the world price, 40 of which is domestic value added and 60 is an imported input. A 20 percent tariff is placed on the finished good and a 10 percent tariff on the imported input. What is the effective rate of protection on domestic value added, in percent? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Protected, the finished good sells for 120 and the input costs 66, so value added is 120 minus 66, which is 54 against the unprotected 40. The effective rate is the change in value added over the original value added, 54 minus 40 over 40, which is 35 percent. The second route writes the same calculation as a closed form: the change in value added is the finished good tariff revenue on the gross value, 100 times 0.2, that is 20, less the extra cost of the input, 60 times 0.1, that is 6, and 14 over 40 is again 35 percent. Quoting the 20 percent final tariff or the 10 percent input tariff would ignore that protection is a differential between the two, and leaving out the finished good tariff would give a fall of 6 in value added, that is minus 15 percent.
questions.hint: Price the finished good and the input at the protected prices, then divide the change in value added by the original value added.

questions.explanation: The producer buys the input on the domestic market, so an input tariff enters its cost of production, and if the finished good price is set by the finished good tariff and by foreign competition, the input cost is not recovered. The effective rate of protection is the difference between the two tariff rates adjusted for the share of inputs in the cost, so a positive tariff on inputs lowers the effective protection and can make it negative. This is why industrial policy in countries that tax imported inputs tends to hurt the export industries, which face input tariffs without any offsetting finished good tariff at all.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: An import quota as an equivalent tariff
questions.learningObjective: compute the tariff equivalent to an import quota from demand and supply slopes
questions.stem: A good is imported at a free trade price of 10, and at that price 80 units are consumed and 50 produced, so imports are 30. Consumption falls by 2 units for each unit the price rises and domestic production rises by 3 units. A quota of 18 units a year is imposed. What tariff, as a percentage of the free trade price, is equivalent to that quota?

options.text: 40 percent, because the quota removes 12 of 30 units of imports and 12 over 30 is 40 percent
options.misconception: converts the fall in the import volume straight into a proportional tariff without any price slopes

options.text: 60 percent, because the 12 unit fall in imports divided by the demand slope of 2 gives a price rise of 6
options.misconception: ignores the response of domestic production, which also absorbs part of the cut in imports

options.text: 24 percent, because the 12 unit fall in imports divided by the two slopes of 5 gives a rise of 2.4, or 24 percent of 10
120 percent, because imports fall by 12 units and 12 units against a price of 10 is a change of 120 percent
options.misconception: treats a change in a quantity as if it were a change in the price, and drops both slopes

questions.explanation: The quota cuts imports from 30 to 18, a fall of 12 units, and the change in imports is the sum of the two responses, 2 plus 3 for every unit of price, which is 5 units, so the price has to rise by 12 over 5, that is 2.4. As a percentage of the free trade price of 10 that is 24 percent. Substituting back confirms it: at a price of 12.4, consumption is 80 minus 2 times 2.4, which is 75.2, production is 50 plus 3 times 2.4, which is 57.2, and the imports are 75.2 minus 57.2, that is 18 as the quota requires. Reading 40 percent would convert the fall in import volume straight into a proportional tariff, and 60 percent would use only the demand response.
questions.hint: The change in imports equals the two slopes times the price change, so solve for the price change and then divide by the free trade price.

questions.topic: Where the rents from a quota go

questions.stem: The quota equivalent is a 24 percent tariff on an import price of 10, so the price wedge is 2.4 a unit, and the quota holds imports at 18 units a year. What is the annual value of the rents created by the quota, before any of it is spent on obtaining the licence?

options.misconception: applies the price wedge to the pre-quota import volume that the quota no longer collects revenue on

options.text: 2.4, the wedge itself, since the rent is the difference between the two prices rather than a total
options.misconception: reports the price difference per unit and leaves out the number of units it applies to

options.text: 18, the number of units the quota allows in, since that is the volume over which a rent is earned
options.misconception: reports the permitted volume and ignores that the rent is a price wedge rather than a quantity

options.text: 43.2, being the wedge of 2.4 on each of the 18 units the quota still allows in

questions.explanation: The rent is the wedge between the domestic price and the world price on the units that are actually imported, so it is 2.4 times 18, which is 43.2 a year. The same figure can be read as the tariff revenue a 24 percent tariff would have raised on the same volume, since a quota and its equivalent tariff deliver the same domestic price; the difference is only who receives the money. With a tariff the state collects all 43.2, whereas with a quota the licence holders collect it unless allocation is competitive or the state auctions the licences, in which case the auction revenue is the rent. Using the pre-quota volume of 30 would give 72, which is the revenue of a tariff that the quota no longer collects.
questions.hint: Multiply the price wedge by the volume of imports the quota allows.

questions.topic: Trade creation in a customs union
questions.learningObjective: state when a customs union raises welfare through trade creation
questions.stem: A customs union removes tariffs on trade between its members and applies a common external tariff to non-members. Under what condition does the union create trade rather than merely divert it?

options.text: When the common external tariff is low enough that members' goods are still the cheapest source after it is applied
When the members' goods are the cheapest at any price, so the external tariff never changes the sourcing decision
options.misconception: removes the external tariff from the calculation, which is exactly the part that can cause diversion

options.text: When the union sets no external tariff at all, so that no non-member can ever undercut a member
options.misconception: demands the absence of an external tariff, which would remove the source of the loss as well

options.text: When every member produces both goods the other member produces, so no trade needs to change hands
options.misconception: rules out intra-union trade, which is the channel through which creation operates

questions.explanation: Removing the tariff between members can only help if members' goods were previously taxed, because an untaxed good that nobody buys was not being kept out by a tariff. What decides the outcome is the common external tariff: if it is high enough to make a non-member's goods cheaper than a member's, purchases move out of the union and welfare falls even though the members' tariffs are gone. The condition for creation is that the external tariff is set low enough for the union to remain the cheapest source, which is a general point about any trade arrangement that replaces several national tariffs with one common one.

questions.stem: Before forming a customs union, country A buys 40 units a year from country B at 8 each and 20 units from country C at 10 each, with no tariff on either. The union removes the tariff on B's goods and imposes a 5 percent common external tariff, so C's goods now cost 10.50 while B's still cost 8. Suppose A then switches 12 units of its purchases from C to B. How large is the deadweight loss from trade diversion, in money units? Report the number only.

The loss is that 0.50 on the 8 units that remain, which is 4. The second route is the import bill: it was 40 times 8 plus 20 times 10, that is 520, and afterwards it is 52 times 8 plus 8 times 10.50, that is 500, a fall of 20; of that fall, 12 times 2 is 24 of genuine consumer gain and 8 times 0.50 is 4 of loss, and 24 minus 4 is the 20 the bill shows. The trap is to apply the wedge to the 12 switched units, which would be a gain rather than a loss because those units come from the cheaper source.
questions.hint: The loss is the common external tariff on the units still bought from outside the union.

options.text: It limits how many different goods a member may export to another member without a licence
options.misconception: describes a quantitative restriction on trade volumes rather than an origin test

options.text: It requires members to withdraw any domestic subsidy for exports shipped to another member
options.misconception: confuses an origin test with a prohibition on the use of export subsidies

options.text: It specifies how much processing a product must undergo in a member before it qualifies for the preferential rate

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The infant industry argument
questions.learningObjective: state the infant industry argument and the conditions under which it holds
questions.stem: The infant industry argument is that a government should protect a young industry from foreign competition until it can compete. What has to be true for the protection to raise national income rather than to move income between consumers and producers?

answer.exemplar: Protection has to buy something that the market would not otherwise supply: learning by doing, a scale economy that is only reachable once output is large, or a spillover from research to other firms. If the industry can reach the learning curve on its own once it is large enough, and if the policy that expands its output is temporary and credible, then the protected period can leave the industry with lower unit costs after protection ends and the welfare gain is the value of the externality, discounted by the cost of the protection used to buy it. If any of the three conditions fails the protection is simply a permanent transfer from consumers to the industry's owners: the learning does not happen, the tariff outlives the argument for it, or the externality was never there to be internalised.

questions.explanation: A tariff's normal incidence is a transfer, so an argument for one has to identify a wedge between the private and the social return, and the argument's whole content is what that wedge is. Timing is the other half, because an infant industry that is protected for ten years has not been tested by the market when the tariff is removed, and a government that cannot commit to removing it is running a transfer scheme. The comparison to make is the value of the externality against the cost of the protection, and a calculation that reports the externality without the cost is the usual way the argument is misused.
questions.hint: Ask what the tariff buys that the market would not have paid for, and when it stops.

questions.topic: The optimum tariff
questions.learningObjective: state the marginal condition for the optimal tariff and its dependence on elasticities
questions.stem: The terms of trade argument for a tariff depends on how elastic importers are and how elastic foreign suppliers are. Which statements about the size of the optimal tariff are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: If foreign suppliers face perfectly elastic export supply, the optimal tariff is zero, since no tariff can move their price
The more elastic a country's import demand, the smaller the optimal tariff, because a larger tariff destroys more trade
The optimal tariff is a single fixed number that holds for every large country regardless of how either side responds
options.misconception: supposes the optimum is independent of the elasticities, which are what determine how the two sides respond

options.text: The optimal tariff is the rate that maximises the deadweight loss, since the loss is what the price wedge is designed to produce
options.misconception: maximises the distortion, which is the cost side of the calculation rather than the benefit side

questions.explanation: The whole gain available to a large country comes from moving the price its suppliers accept, so if supply is perfectly elastic there is nothing to be gained and the optimal tariff is zero, which is exactly the small country case. The more elastic import demand is, the more volume a given wedge removes, so the distortion cost rises faster than the terms of trade gain and the optimal rate falls; the first order approximation makes it fall as the reciprocal of the sum of the two elasticities, which is why the commonly quoted answer is a small positive number for finite elasticities. Neither a fixed number nor a rate that maximises the loss can be right, since the loss and the gain move in opposite directions and the optimum is where they are equal.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the gain if the foreign price cannot move, and what happens to the cost if a wedge removes a lot of trade.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Strategic trade policy with increasing returns
questions.learningObjective: explain the logic of strategic trade policy under increasing returns
questions.stem: Strategic trade policy is used to say that a government should help domestic firms in industries with increasing returns to scale. What must be true of the world market for that recommendation to have a chance of working?

answer.exemplar: The world market has to be concentrated enough that one firm's output decisions move world prices, so that being the first mover in a narrow window is worth a subsidy. With a few firms of significant size in a small number of industries, being established in an industry can lock in a position that later entrants cannot easily take, and a subsidy that shifts the timing of investment can capture that position. The result follows immediately: since the number of industries is small, subsidising all of them cannot work, so the government has to pick winners, and the argument becomes a claim about the quality of the government's information rather than about the tariff. Where world markets are unconcentrated, scale economies are internal, competition squeezes margins towards cost, and the strategic argument has no purchase at all.

questions.explanation: The whole argument rests on market concentration, because the profit that a subsidy can protect has to come from a price that the firm's own output affects. Without concentration the price equals the cost of the marginal producer, profits are competed away, and a subsidy is a pure transfer. The policy conclusion is uncomfortable and is the reason the argument is treated with caution in most assessments: it implies picking a small number of industries, which requires the state to know which of the industries in the world are the ones where a subsidy changes the outcome, and that is a claim about the quality of state information, not about the level of the tariff.
questions.hint: Ask whether one firm's output can move the world price of its own product.

questions.topic: The budget cost of an export subsidy
questions.learningObjective: compute the cost of an export subsidy and the loss it produces
questions.stem: A small country produces 100 million units of a good and consumes 50 at a world price of 4, so it exports 50. A subsidy of 20 percent of the world price, that is 0.80 a unit, is paid on every unit exported and raises the domestic price to 4.80. Production rises to 110 and consumption falls to 35. What does the subsidy cost the government, and what is the net loss to the country? Give the two amounts in that order.

options.text: 60 and 10, since exports rise to 75 and the loss is the production and consumption distortion of 4 plus 6
40 and 10, counting only the 50 units that were exported before the subsidy was introduced
options.misconception: pays the subsidy on the pre-policy export volume instead of on the volume actually exported

options.text: 60 and 0, on the argument that the extra output is exported so nothing is wasted and the cost is paid abroad
options.misconception: treats the extra output as a free gain and ignores the higher cost of the units consumers now buy

options.text: 60 and 20, counting the consumption distortion twice because consumers lose on both the extra and the lost units
options.misconception: double counts the consumption distortion of 6, which is already part of the 10

questions.explanation: Exports rise to 110 less 35, that is 75 million units, and the subsidy is 0.80 on each, so the budget cost is 60. The loss to consumers is half the 0.80 wedge times the 85 units they now buy, which is 34, and the gain to producers is half the wedge times the 210 units now made, which is 84, so the net effect is minus 34 plus 84 minus 60, that is minus 10. The second route is the two triangles, 4 on the 10 units of extra production and 6 on the 15 units of forgone consumption, which is the same 10. That the two agree is the check that the subsidy is not a free gain: it moves output towards a producer whose cost is higher than the world price.
questions.hint: Exports are production less consumption after the policy; the loss is the sum of the two triangles.

questions.topic: Retaliation and the terms of trade
questions.learningObjective: explain why a terms of trade argument does not survive retaliation
questions.stem: A large country argues that a tariff improves its terms of trade, so why does the argument usually fail once retaliation is allowed for?

options.text: Retaliation leaves the first country's terms of trade untouched, because a tariff on its exports cannot change the price it receives
options.misconception: denies that restricting a country's exports changes the price that country receives

options.text: A retaliating partner restricts the first country's exports, which improves the first country's terms of trade by about as much as its tariff damaged the partner's
Retaliation raises the first country's terms of trade, because its partner now has less to sell and so bids less for what is left
options.misconception: reverses the sign, since less supply to sell means a higher, not a lower, price for the goods

options.text: Retaliation converts the tariff into an import quota, and a quota cannot improve the terms of trade
options.misconception: replaces one instrument with another when the issue is the price effect, not the instrument

questions.explanation: A tariff improves the terms of trade by making foreign producers cut the price they accept, and the first country's own exports are what a retaliating tariff restricts. The retaliation therefore works on the same mechanism in the opposite direction, and when the two countries are of comparable size the second gain largely cancels the first, leaving the distortion losses on both sides. What survives is the small-country case, where the country's imports are too small to move the price and no terms of trade is available to begin with, so a large country that wants the argument has to believe retaliation will not arrive.

options.misconception: converts a delay measured in days into a fraction of a year by using the number of days as months

options.text: 0.167 percent, being 10 percent for one sixtieth of a year, since 6 of 360 days is one sixtieth
0.6 percent, which is 10 percent of 6, treating the 6 days as though it were a fraction of 100 days
options.misconception: multiplies the annual rate by the raw number of days instead of by the fraction of the year

options.text: 2 percent, which is 10 percent of 6 of 30 days, using a month as the length of the year
options.misconception: divides by 30 instead of by 360, so the delay is treated as two months of financing cost

questions.explanation: Capital is tied up for 6 of the 360 days, so the fraction of a year is 6 over 360, that is one sixtieth, and the cost is that fraction times the annual rate, 0.10 over 60, which is 0.001667, or 0.167 percent of the shipment's value. questions.topic: The resource cost of seeking quota rents
questions.learningObjective: compute the resource cost of competition for quota rents
questions.stem: An import quota creates rents of 43.2 a year, being a price wedge of 2.4 on the 18 units that are still imported. Applicants compete for the licences and a third of all resources spent in doing so goes to the officials who allocate them, with the rest dissipated among the applicants. What is the annual resource cost of the rent seeking? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Rent seeking absorbs the whole of the rent that competition cannot capture, so the resource cost is 43.2 in the limit, and the fraction that officials capture is still a real resource cost because it consumes labour and effort that could be used elsewhere. questions.topic: Balance of payments double entry

A matching entry of 300 appears in the financial account, because the country's foreign assets rise by the unpaid claim created
The two entries are equal and opposite, so the sum of all accounts before the reserves and the errors item is zero
Only the credit is recorded, because the buyer pays from abroad and the payment is not a domestic transaction

options.misconception: moves primary income into the financial account, where it is not recorded

options.text: Primary income and transfers only, since the trade balance belongs to the national accounts of exports
options.misconception: omits the trade balance, which is the largest and best known part of the current account

options.text: Trade in goods and services, net primary income from abroad, and net secondary income, that is transfers
All external transactions of any kind, including direct investment and portfolio flows

The financial account records changes in the stock of foreign assets and liabilities, so direct and portfolio investment belong there. Keeping the two apart is what makes the current account interpretable, because a deficit on it says the country is consuming more than it is earning, and the financial account says who is financing the difference.

questions.stem: A country's current account is a deficit of 60. What is the total of the financial account, and does the balance of payments close?
questions.explanation: The financial account is the sum of the flows with reserves signed the other way, because a fall in reserve assets is an increase in the country's foreign assets and so is a credit, giving 60 plus 30 plus 15 minus 45, that is 60. The current account deficit of 60 and the financial account surplus of 60 cancel exactly, so the accounts close with nothing left over, which is the test that the sign conventions have been applied consistently. The reading that matters for policy is that a 60 inflow of direct investment plus 45 of reserves drawn down financed the deficit, so the financing was partly hot and partly a loss of the country's buffer.

questions.explanation: The two accounts sum to plus 4, since minus 60 plus 64 is 4, and the balance of payments has to sum to zero, so the residual is minus 4. A negative residual means the recorded inflows exceed the recorded outflows by 4, which is the normal sign when unrecorded capital outflow exceeds unrecorded inflow, as with cash carried across a border or a payment routed through a third country. A rise in the holdings when a foreign government lends funds directly to the central bank
A fall in the holdings when residents convert domestic deposits into foreign currency at a bank

questions.learningObjective: trace the monetary base through a purchase of foreign currency and a sterilising sale
questions.stem: A central bank's monetary base is 200. It buys 10 of foreign currency from a resident bank, paying with domestic currency, so the base rises. It then sells 10 of its own securities to that same bank to take the domestic currency back out. What is the base immediately after the purchase, and what is it after the sale?

options.misconception: holds that a sale of securities adds to the base, whereas it withdraws the currency the purchase created

options.text: 200 then 200, because buying foreign currency does not change the base until the currency is withdrawn again
options.misconception: ignores the intermediate stage, in which the base is 10 higher while the domestic currency is outstanding

options.text: 220 then 210, because the base rises by the 200 of reserves and the securities, not by the traded amount alone

options.text: 210 then 200, because the sale of securities removes exactly the domestic currency the purchase created

That composition change is the whole content of a sterilised intervention: the central bank has altered the currency in which its assets are denominated without altering the quantity of base money, and therefore without altering the money stock, which is why the exchange rate can move while the domestic interest rate need not.

questions.explanation: The current account is debited with all the income earned by foreign owners, whether or not it is paid out, so it is the 20 remitted plus the 15 reinvested, that is 35. The second route is the double entry: the 15 of reinvested earnings is an acquisition of a foreign liability of 15, which appears in the financial account as an inward flow, and the corresponding credit is a primary income outflow, so the same 15 appears once in each account while the current account records 35. Treating reinvested earnings as a financial flow only would understate the income outflow, and a country whose recorded inward investment exceeds its recorded income outflows is likely to be recording retained earnings too lightly.
questions.hint: Add the profits that leave the country to the earnings that are earned there but reinvested.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Foreign ownership of domestic assets
questions.learningObjective: compute the cost of a depreciation to foreign holders of domestic debt
questions.stem: Output is 1,600 and the stock of domestic government bonds is 800, of which foreign residents hold 40 percent. The currency depreciates by 20 percent, and the foreign holders suffer a valuation loss on the principal of the bonds they hold, measured in domestic currency. What is that loss as a percentage of one year's output? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Foreign holders have 0.4 times 800, that is 320, of the stock, and a 20 percent depreciation revalues that principal by 0.20 times 320, which is 64, and 64 over 1,600 is 4 percent of one year's output. The second route is the ratio of the foreign share of the debt to output times the depreciation, 320 over 1,600 is 0.2, times 0.2 is 0.04, which is the same 4 percent. The item is about the stock and not the flow, so it says nothing about interest payments, which would be a further income outflow in the same direction; the comparison that matters is between the size of the foreign share of the debt and the size of the country's own external assets, which is the balance sheet that determines who is exposed.
questions.hint: Find the foreign-held principal, revalue it at the depreciation, and divide by output.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Import penetration
questions.learningObjective: compute import penetration and distinguish it from other ratios
questions.stem: A country imports manufactured goods worth 300 a year. Its output is 1,000, of which 600 is manufactured. What is the import penetration ratio of manufactures, in percent?

options.text: 30 percent, which is the 300 imported against total output of 1,000 including services and farming
options.misconception: divides the imports by total output rather than by the domestic output of the good being imported

options.text: 33.3 percent, which is the 300 imported against imports plus domestic output of 900
options.misconception: adds the imports to domestic supply and so counts the imported units as if they were domestic

options.text: 60 percent, which is the 600 of domestic manufacturing output against total output of 1,000
options.misconception: computes the domestic share of manufacturing and reports it as though it were a penetration rate

options.text: 50 percent, which is the 300 imported against the 600 of domestic manufacturing output

questions.explanation: Import penetration is imports of a good divided by that good's domestic output, so 300 over 600, which is 0.5, that is 50 percent. The second route rules out the two neighbouring ratios: imports over total output is 300 over 1,000, that is 30 percent, which is the share of the economy that imports, and imports over imports plus domestic output is 300 over 900, that is 33.3 percent, which counts the imports as if they were domestic supply. The distinction matters for policy, because a penetration rate of 50 percent says half of domestic demand is met from abroad while the same 300 is only 30 percent of the economy as a whole.
questions.hint: Divide the imports of the good by the domestic output of that same good, not by total output.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why an export-led strategy is vulnerable to a terms of trade reversal
questions.learningObjective: explain the exposure created by concentrating production in one export sector
questions.stem: An export-led strategy has a country raise its growth rate by expanding one labour-intensive export sector that earns foreign currency. What is the structural exposure that creates, and how does it differ from the exposure of a country that exports a varied basket?

answer.exemplar: Concentration makes the country's real income a lever on one price, because a specialised exporter has no second product to sell when the price of its one export falls. A 10 percent fall in the export price against an unchanged import price is a terms of trade loss worth the exported share of output, and the loss is not offset anywhere else, so the same shock that a diversified exporter absorbs across many prices arrives at the concentrated one whole. The exposure compounds through the exchange rate and the debt: the currency earned by the single sector is what services foreign borrowing, so a price fall simultaneously cuts income and raises the domestic cost of that debt, and the country may have to deflate wages to stay competitive. A varied basket is not immune, since prices move together, but no single price move carries the whole economy, and the gains from a boom in one sector are not all spent on the imports that the next downturn makes expensive.

questions.explanation: A specialised exporter's real income is the product of its output per worker and the price of its single export, so the price enters with a coefficient of one and there is no second term to offset it. Concentration also links the exchange rate, the wage and the external debt into one adjustment, because the foreign currency from the sector is what services the debt and a fall in its price makes that service dearer in domestic currency. The response, which is to hold the exchange rate and cut the domestic wage, converts a terms of trade loss into a deflation, and that is the point at which a strategy that raised growth also lowered living standards.
questions.hint: Ask what a specialised exporter has to sell when the world price of its one good falls.
